context: Both routes start with [7, 3, 2, 6, 0, 1, 5, 4] and aim for [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. For an array of length n, the figure compares the work before and after splitting using complexity expressions. It gives no measured running times.
description: The left route runs bubble sort on the full array of length n, labeled O(n²), and outputs the ascending array [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] at the bottom.

The right route splits at the midpoint into [7, 3, 2, 6] and [0, 1, 5, 4], labeled “Split O(n).” Each half of length n/2 is sorted separately, labeled “Bubble sort O((n/2)²),” giving [2, 3, 6, 7] and [0, 1, 4, 5]. The final step, “Merge O(n),” repeatedly takes the smaller available element from the two halves to form [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

Crossing arrows in the merge step show that elements from the two sorted halves must be interleaved by value. Simply concatenating the halves would not sort the array. The bottom label “Overall O(n²/2 + 2n)” accounts for two half-size bubble sorts plus linear splitting and merging.

frames.explanation: After one split, O(n²/2 + 2n) is still asymptotically O(n²). The simplified expression illustrates the potential benefit of a smaller quadratic coefficient. It gives neither an exact operation count nor a guarantee of halving the running time.
frames.title: Splitting one bubble sort into two smaller sorts

summary: Bubble sorting eight elements directly and sorting the two halves separately before merging give the same result. A single split still leaves quadratic time complexity.
title: Splitting one bubble sort into two smaller sorts
